# Where one cross-section runs out {.divider background-color="#008CB7"}

[Act I · The tension]{.act}

::: {.notes}
This is the capstone chapter. Chapters 1–16 fitted regressions to cross-sections: one observation per unit, no ordering. Real economic data usually has more structure: the same units observed repeatedly (panels), observations ordered in time (time series), and regressors that are themselves chosen (endogeneity). Each structure changes what a slope means and how uncertain it is.
:::

## A slope is only as good as the variation behind it

A regression slope compares observations. With **one cross-section**, the only comparison is *across* units: big-market teams versus small-market teams, rich countries versus poor ones. Whatever else differs between them rides along in the slope.

. . .

This chapter adds two new sources of variation and one warning:

- **Panel data**: the same unit over time, so we can compare a unit *with itself*
- **Time series**: one unit, many periods, so we must respect *order and memory*
- **Causation**: no amount of structure helps if the regressor is correlated with the error

[The question running through the whole deck: *which variation identifies this coefficient*, and which standard error is honest about it?]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Frame the deck around one question. Pooled OLS uses all variation; fixed effects uses only within-unit variation; first differences uses only period-to-period changes; levels regressions with trending series may be identified by nothing more than two shared trends. The standard error has to match the dependence in the data: clustered for panels, HAC for time series.
:::

## Three data structures, three new problems {.smaller}

| Data | Structure | Size | What goes wrong with plain OLS |
|:---------|:--------|:--------|:--------------------|
| `AED_NBA.DTA` | team × season | 29 teams, 286 obs. | errors correlated within a team; team traits confound the slope |
| `AED_EARNINGS_COMPLETE.DTA` | cross-section, 0/1 outcome | 872 workers | a straight line predicts "probabilities" outside $[0,1]$ |
| `AED_INTERESTRATES.DTA` | monthly time series | 397 months | trends fake a relationship; errors are autocorrelated |
| Mendez (2020) | country × year | 108 × 25 | country traits confound capital's slope |
| DS4Bolivia | municipality × year | 339 × 9 | municipality traits confound population's slope |

[Each structure needs two fixes: one for the **coefficient** (which variation) and one for the **standard error** (which dependence).]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's datasets list says 842 workers; the data file loads 872 observations, and every result in the chapter uses all 872. The NBA panel is unbalanced: 28 teams for 10 seasons plus the Bobcats for 6, so 286 team-seasons, not 290.
:::

## One estimator, four ways to be honest about uncertainty {.smaller}

| SE type | pyfixest syntax | Allows errors to be… | Used for |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Default (iid) | *(none)* | independent, equal variance | benchmark only |
| Heteroskedasticity-robust | `vcov="HC1"` | independent, unequal variance | earnings LPM / logit |
| Cluster-robust | `vcov={"CRV1": "teamid"}` | correlated **within** a cluster, independent across | NBA, CS 1, CS 2 |
| HAC (Newey–West) | `vcov="NW"`, `vcov_kwargs={"time_id": ..., "lag": 24}` | correlated across nearby **periods** | interest rates |

[The coefficient never changes with `vcov`; only SEs, $t$, $p$ and CIs do. In this deck the honest SE is 1.8× (NBA), 4× (countries) and 3.65× (rates) the default.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
pf.feols is the only estimator for linear models in this chapter; the logit uses statsmodels. The vcov argument changes only inference. Cluster-robust SEs allow any correlation pattern among the observations of one team (or country, or municipality), so they cover both persistent team effects and serial correlation within a team. Newey–West SEs allow correlation that dies out after a chosen number of lags (24 months here).
:::

## The thread: which variation identifies the slope?

::: {.incremental}
- **Pooled OLS** uses *all* variation: between units **and** within units over time
- **Between** variation: differences in unit averages (Knicks vs Bucks)
- **Within** variation: a unit's deviations from its own average (the Lakers' good vs bad seasons). **Fixed effects use only this**
- **Changes** ($\Delta y_t$ on $\Delta x_t$): period-to-period movements. **First differences** and time-series regressions in changes use only this
- **Levels of two trending series**: may be identified by little more than two shared trends, the classic *spurious* regression
:::

[When a coefficient changes as we move from one kind of variation to another, the change itself is evidence about confounding.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is the deck's recurring thread. We will see it four times: NBA (0.0068 pooled → 0.0045 within), countries (capital elasticity 0.71 → 0.44), Bolivian municipalities (population slope +0.34 → −0.82), and interest rates (levels vs changes). Each change is a diagnostic for confounding by something time-invariant (panels) or by a common trend (time series).
:::

## Six ideas anchor this chapter

::: {.incremental}
- **Panel data**: observations indexed by unit $i$ *and* time $t$
- **Within estimator**: subtract each unit's own mean to erase its fixed traits $\alpha_i$
- **Logit**: push $x'\beta$ through an S-curve so probabilities stay in $[0,1]$
- **AR($p$)**: regress $y_t$ on its own past values; persistence and momentum
- **ADL**: add current and lagged $x$; cumulative sums of the $\gamma$'s trace the dynamic effect
- **Hausman test**: compares FE and RE; a significant gap rejects RE's assumption
:::

[Each idea answers the same question under harder conditions: *what is really driving $y$?*]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
These are the chapter's Key Concepts. One caution: the Hausman test appears in the Key Concepts and Key Takeaways, but the chapter never estimates random effects or runs the test. The deck presents it as a concept (17.4), not as a result.
:::

# 17.2 · Do wins raise NBA team revenue? {#sec-panel .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Panel structure · within vs between · pooled OLS · cluster-robust SEs]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 17.2: the NBA panel. Tools: describing a panel, decomposing variation, pooled OLS, and why default SEs are wrong when the same team appears ten times.
:::

## The question and the panel {.smaller}

**Data.** NBA team finances, 2001–02 to 2010–11 (`AED_NBA.DTA`): **29 teams, 286 team-seasons**. Revenue is in millions of dollars.

| Variable | Meaning | Mean | Range |
|:--|:--|--:|:--|
| `revenue` | team revenue, \$ millions | 95.7 | 58.5 – 187.7 |
| `lnrevenue` | log revenue (outcome) | 4.532 | 4.069 – 5.235 |
| `wins` | regular-season wins (of 82) | 41.0 | 9 – 67 |
| `playoff` | 1 if the team made the playoffs | 0.545 | 0 – 1 |
| `teamid`, `season` | the two panel indexes $i$ and $t$ | | 29 teams × up to 10 seasons |

[The panel is **unbalanced**: 28 teams appear in all 10 seasons, the Bobcats in only 6, so $N = 286$, not $29 \times 10 = 290$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Economic question: does winning raise a team's revenue? A team that wins more sells more tickets, merchandise and playoff games. But big-market teams also have more money to buy winning rosters, so the association could run both ways.

The chapter's cluster-SE discussion says "29 teams × 10 years = 290 independent observations"; the data have 286.
:::

## Three ways to use a panel

$$y_{it} = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x_{it} + u_{it}, \qquad i = 1,\dots,n \;(\text{teams}),\; t = 1,\dots,T \;(\text{seasons})$$

::: {.incremental}
- **Pooled OLS**: ignore the panel structure in estimation; fix the SEs by **clustering on $i$**
- **Fixed effects (FE)**: give each unit its own intercept, $y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_2 x_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}$, and estimate $\beta_2$ from **within-unit** changes only
- **Random effects (RE)**: treat $\alpha_i$ as a random draw, $u_{it} = \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}$, assumed **uncorrelated with $x$**; uses a weighted mix of within and between variation
:::

[The three estimators differ in *which comparison* they make, not in arithmetic sophistication.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Pooled OLS treats each team-season as a separate observation for the coefficient but must cluster for inference. FE allows the team effect to be correlated with wins (big markets win more) because it never compares one team with another. RE is more efficient but only consistent if the team effect is unrelated to the regressor.
:::

## Code: load the panel and inspect its structure

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-6|7-8|9"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                     # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import numpy as np                           # numerical operations
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                        # OLS / fixed effects with robust and cluster SEs
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_NBA.DTA"
data_nba = pd.read_stata(url)                # one row per team-season
print(data_nba.shape)                        # (286, 65): rows, columns
print(data_nba.groupby("teamid").size().value_counts())   # seasons observed per team
data_nba[["revenue", "lnrevenue", "wins", "playoff"]].describe().round(3)
```

::: {.notes}
Self-contained: paste into an empty Colab cell. The value_counts line reveals the unbalanced panel: 28 teams with 10 seasons, one team (the Bobcats, an expansion franchise) with 6.
:::

## Code: split the variation into between and within

$$\underbrace{y_{it}-\bar y}_{\text{overall}} \;=\; \underbrace{\bar y_i-\bar y}_{\text{between}} \;+\; \underbrace{y_{it}-\bar y_i}_{\text{within}}$$

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|3-6|7"}
# continues from the previous block
g = data_nba.groupby("teamid")                      # group the rows by team
for v in ["lnrevenue", "wins"]:
    overall = data_nba[v].std()                     # SD over all 286 team-seasons
    between = g[v].mean().std()                     # SD of the 29 team averages
    within = (data_nba[v] - g[v].transform("mean")).std()   # SD of deviations from own mean
    print(f"{v:10s} overall {overall:.4f}  between {between:.4f}  within {within:.4f}")
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
The decomposition is exact for sums of squares. With standard deviations it holds approximately, because the between SD is computed over 29 team means and the within SD over 286 deviations. The chapter computes this only in its cheat-sheet block; it is the first thing to run on any panel.
:::

## Output: revenue varies across teams, wins vary within teams {.smaller}

| Variable | Overall SD | Between SD | Within SD | Share of variance |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| `lnrevenue` | 0.2360 | [0.2127]{.key} | 0.1085 | between ≈ 81% |
| `wins` | 12.44 | 7.04 | [10.36]{.key} | within ≈ 69% |

[Shares: between variance ÷ overall variance (0.0452 / 0.0557) and within variance ÷ overall variance (107.3 / 154.7).]{.comment}

::: {.incremental}
- **Revenue is mostly a team trait**: Knicks average \$162M, Lakers \$150M; Bucks \$70M, Grizzlies \$74M
- **Wins are mostly a season-to-season story**: a team's wins swing more around its own average than team averages differ from each other
:::

[Fixed effects throw away 81% of the revenue variance but keep 69% of the wins variance, so the within estimator still has plenty to work with.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's "~0.21 between, ~0.11 within, ~0.24 overall" is confirmed exactly. What the chapter does not show is the decomposition for wins, and it matters: if wins had almost no within variation, FE estimates would be very imprecise. Here they have plenty.

The chapter's text uses illustrative revenue figures (Lakers "~$300M", Grizzlies "$150M", a "$200M+" gap). In this sample the Lakers average $150.5M and the Grizzlies $73.7M; the largest gap between team averages (Knicks $162.2M vs Bucks $70.5M) is about $92M.
:::

## Between and within, side by side

![Left: one dot per team (its 10-season averages). Right: each team-season as a deviation from its own team average, with the fixed-effects slope.](figures/fig_nba_between_within.png)

[The left panel mixes market size with winning (the Knicks earn the most while winning few games). The right panel compares each team only with itself.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Left: across teams the relationship is noisy; the Knicks and Bulls earn a lot without winning much, because of market size. Team-average revenue and team-average wins correlate only 0.40. Right: after removing each team's averages, more wins than usual go with more revenue than usual. This is exactly the variation fixed effects use; the yellow line is the FE slope, 0.0045.
:::

## The pooled picture mixes both comparisons

![Each dot is a team-season. The pooled OLS line runs through between-team and within-team differences at once.](figures/fig_x_01.png)

[The pooled slope partly credits winning for market size: big-market teams sit high on the revenue axis whatever their record.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is the chapter's Figure 17.1. The positive slope is real as a description, but it bundles two comparisons. The next code block estimates it and asks how to compute its standard error.
:::

## Code: pooled OLS with three kinds of standard errors

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-6|7"}
# continues from the previous block
f_iid = pf.feols("lnrevenue ~ wins", data=data_nba)                 # default (iid) SEs
f_hc1 = pf.feols("lnrevenue ~ wins", data=data_nba, vcov="HC1")     # heteroskedasticity-robust
fit_pool = pf.feols("lnrevenue ~ wins", data=data_nba, vcov={"CRV1": "teamid"})  # by team
for name, f in [("default", f_iid), ("HC1", f_hc1), ("cluster", fit_pool)]:
    print(name, f.coef()["wins"], f.se()["wins"], f.tstat()["wins"])   # same b, new SE
fit_pool.summary()                           # full table with cluster-robust SEs
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Three fits of the same model. pyfixest's default for a model without fixed effects is iid SEs. HC1 allows heteroskedasticity across observations. CRV1 with teamid allows any correlation among the ten observations of one team.
:::

## Output: same slope, very different uncertainty {.smaller}

| SE type | Coef. on `wins` | SE | $t$ | $p$ | 95% CI | SE ÷ default |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|--:|
| Default (iid) | 0.00675 | 0.00105 | 6.42 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.00468,&nbsp;0.00882] | 1.00 |
| HC1 | 0.00675 | 0.00102 | 6.61 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.00474,&nbsp;0.00876] | 0.97 |
| Cluster by team | 0.00675 | [0.00191]{.key} | 3.54 | 0.001 | [0.00284,&nbsp;0.01066] | [1.81]{.key} |

[N = 286 · 29 clusters · $R^2 = 0.127$ (identical in all three rows)]{.comment}

[Heteroskedasticity is not the problem here (HC1 ≈ default). **Within-team dependence** is: allowing for it widens the SE by 81% and halves the $t$-statistic.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Reproduces the chapter's table: default 0.0011, robust 0.0010, cluster 0.0019, ratio 1.81. The chapter elsewhere says cluster SEs are "2x or more" and that clustering "roughly doubles" the SE; in this example the factor is 1.81. Significance survives (t = 3.54, p = 0.001), so clustering corrects the uncertainty without overturning the result.
:::

## Why clustering: ten seasons of one team are not ten independent facts {.smaller}

$$\widehat{V}_{\text{CR}}(\hat\beta) = (X'X)^{-1}\Big(\textstyle\sum_{g=1}^{G} X_g'\hat u_g \hat u_g' X_g\Big)(X'X)^{-1}$$

::: {.incremental}
- The middle term sums over **clusters** $g$, so every pair of residuals *within* a team may be correlated; residuals in *different* teams are assumed independent
- **Two sources** of within-team correlation: a persistent team effect (the Lakers' residual is positive every year) and serial correlation (good years follow good years)
- In the limit of perfect correlation, 10 seasons of one team carry the information of 1 observation; the truth lies in between
:::

[Clustering must be done at the level where shocks are shared. With $G = 29$ clusters the $t$ reference has only $G - 1 = 28$ degrees of freedom.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter writes the cluster formula with an ellipsis in the denominator; the sandwich form above is the complete version. Practical cautions from the chapter: with fewer than about 30 clusters, cluster-robust SEs can still be too small; the wild cluster bootstrap is the usual refinement (mentioned, not run). Two-way clustering (team and season) allows common season shocks too; its variance is V_team + V_season − V_team×season.
:::

## Output: the pooled regression, read correctly {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | SE | $t$ | $p$ | 95% CI |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Intercept | 4.25520 | 0.09572 | 44.45 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [4.05912,&nbsp;4.45128] |
| `wins` | [0.00675]{.key} | 0.00191 | 3.54 | 0.001 | [0.00284,&nbsp;0.01066] |

[N = 286 · CRV1 SEs clustered by `teamid` (29 clusters) · $R^2 = 0.127$]{.comment}

::: {.incremental}
- **Log-level model**: one more win goes with $100 \times 0.00675 \approx 0.68\%$ more revenue (a log-point approximation)
- Ten more wins: $100\,(e^{10 \times 0.00675}-1) = 7.0\%$
- $R^2 = 0.127$: wins describe little of the revenue spread, which is mostly team traits
:::

[This is an **association across and within teams**. Teams that win more also tend to be the rich-market teams, so the slope is not yet "the effect of winning".]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Interpretation of a log-level coefficient: 100 × b is the approximate percentage change in revenue per extra win. For larger changes use the exact transformation 100(e^{Δx·b} − 1). The intercept (4.26, i.e. about $70M) is the predicted log revenue at zero wins, an extrapolation outside the data (minimum 9 wins).
:::

# 17.3 · Fixed effects: compare each team only with itself {#sec-fe .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Within transformation · LSDV · what FE absorbs · omitted-variable bias]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 17.3. Fixed effects remove everything about a team that does not change over the decade: market size, arena, brand, ownership, local income (to the extent it is stable).
:::

## The fixed-effects model and the within transformation {.smaller}

$$y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta\,x_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}$$

Average each team's equation over its seasons and subtract:

$$(y_{it}-\bar y_i) = \beta\,(x_{it}-\bar x_i) + (\varepsilon_{it}-\bar\varepsilon_i)$$

::: {.incremental}
- $\alpha_i$ **disappears**: anything constant within a team cannot bias $\hat\beta$, even if it is correlated with $x$
- Same estimate two ways: **LSDV** (one dummy per team) or **de-meaning** then OLS
- Price: coefficients on **time-invariant** regressors cannot be estimated, and only within variation is used
:::

[FE swap the assumption "no omitted variables" for the weaker "no omitted variables *that change over time within a unit*".]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is the key identifying assumption, often called strict exogeneity: the time-varying error must be uncorrelated with the regressor in every period. Team traits that are fixed over ten seasons (market size, arena, history) are absorbed by alpha_i. Anything that changes over time and drives both wins and revenue (a new star, a new arena, a new TV contract) is not.
:::

## Code: fixed effects, and a check by hand

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-5|6-9"}
# continues from the previous block
fit_fe = pf.feols("lnrevenue ~ wins | teamid", data=data_nba,
                  vcov={"CRV1": "teamid"})   # "| teamid" = one intercept per team
fit_fe.summary()                             # within estimator, cluster SEs by team
print(fit_fe._r2_within)                     # share of WITHIN-team variation explained
# check: the same slope from OLS on de-meaned data (the within transformation)
data_nba["dm_lnrev"] = data_nba["lnrevenue"] - g["lnrevenue"].transform("mean")
data_nba["dm_wins"] = data_nba["wins"] - g["wins"].transform("mean")
print(pf.feols("dm_lnrev ~ dm_wins - 1", data=data_nba).coef())   # identical slope
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
The vertical bar in the formula tells pyfixest to absorb team fixed effects. The last three lines show that FE is nothing more than OLS on de-meaned data: the slope matches to every digit. (The SEs of the manual regression would need a degrees-of-freedom correction for the 29 estimated means; pyfixest handles that.)
:::

## Output: the within-team slope is a third smaller {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | SE | $t$ | $p$ | 95% CI |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| `wins` | [0.00451]{.key} | 0.00084 | 5.35 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.00278,&nbsp;0.00623] |

[N = 286 · 29 team fixed effects · CRV1 SEs by `teamid` · within $R^2 = 0.185$ · manual de-meaned OLS slope: 0.00451]{.comment}

| | Pooled OLS | Fixed effects |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Coefficient on `wins` | 0.00675 | [0.00451]{.key} |
| Cluster SE | 0.00191 | 0.00084 |
| $R^2$ | 0.127 (overall) | 0.185 (within) |

[Holding the team fixed, the slope falls by **33%**, and it is estimated *more* precisely: removing team effects removed most of the residual noise.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Matches the chapter: 0.0045, SE 0.0008, t 5.35, within R² 0.185. The two R² values are not comparable: one is overall, one is within. Also note that clustering still matters inside FE: the iid SE of the FE slope is 0.00059, so clustering widens it by a factor of 1.42, reflecting serial correlation that the team effects did not remove.
:::

## One slope inside each team

![Pooled OLS (red) versus team-specific intercepts with a common fixed-effects slope, for four teams.](figures/fig_nba_fe_lines.png)

[Big-market teams (Knicks, Lakers) sit on high lines, small-market teams (Grizzlies, Bucks) on low ones. The pooled line is steeper because it climbs *across* those lines.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Each colored line uses that team's own intercept alpha_i and the common FE slope 0.0045. The pooled line connects low-revenue, low-win teams with high-revenue, high-win teams, and that cross-team comparison is where the extra steepness comes from.
:::

## Why the slope fell: omitted-variable bias, signed

$$\text{plim}\;\hat\beta_{\text{pooled}} = \beta + \gamma\,\frac{\text{Cov}(\alpha_i, x_{it})}{\text{Var}(x_{it})}$$

::: {.incremental}
- $\gamma > 0$: the team effect (market, brand) raises revenue
- $\text{Cov}(\alpha_i, x_{it}) > 0$: rich-market teams also win somewhat more (team-average revenue and wins correlate 0.40)
- So the pooled slope is biased **upward**: 0.00675 vs 0.00451, a gap of 0.00225
:::

[The direction of the change from pooled to FE is exactly what the omitted-variables formula predicts when the omitted trait helps both $x$ and $y$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Same formula as the Phillips-curve case in Chapter 13: bias = (effect of omitted variable on y) × (slope of omitted variable on x). Here the omitted variable is the team fixed effect. FE does not estimate gamma; it removes the term by construction. The 0.40 correlation is between the 29 team averages of log revenue and wins (computed for these slides).
:::

## What one more win is worth

::: {.incremental}
- **Per win**: $100\,(e^{0.00451}-1) = 0.45\%$ more revenue for the same team
- At the sample mean revenue of **\$95.7M**: about **\$0.43M per win**
- **Ten more wins** than the team's usual: $100\,(e^{10 \times 0.00451}-1) = 4.6\%$, about **\$4.4M**
- The pooled slope would have said 7.0% (\$6.7M) for ten wins
:::

[Winning pays, but far less than the cross-section suggests. Market size, not the win column, is where most revenue differences come from.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter evaluates the effect "for a team with $200M revenue" (0.45% × $200M = $900K). No team-season in this sample reaches $200M (maximum $187.7M; mean $95.7M), so the deck evaluates it at the sample mean instead. All conversions use the exact exponential formula.
:::

## What fixed effects can and cannot fix

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Absorbed (time-invariant)**

- market size and local income level
- arena, franchise history, brand
- ownership style (if stable)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Not absorbed (time-varying)**

- a star arrives, a coach changes, injuries
- new arena or TV contract mid-panel
- league-wide shocks (lockouts, recessions)
- revenue → payroll → wins (reverse causality)
:::
::::

[FE make the causal reading *more plausible*, not guaranteed. A natural next step is season fixed effects, `| teamid + season`, for league-wide shocks.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Two fidelity notes. The chapter writes the FE model with a season term (γ·season_t) but its code estimates lnrevenue ~ wins | teamid, without season effects; the slides report what the code estimates. The chapter also illustrates FE with Golden State in 2015 and the Lakers in 2012 and 2015; those seasons are outside this sample (2001–02 to 2010–11). Season fixed effects are suggested as an extension, not estimated here.
:::

# 17.4 · Fixed or random effects? {#sec-re .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Random effects · efficiency vs consistency · the Hausman test]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 17.4. The chapter describes random effects and the Hausman test but does not estimate either: its 17.4 code prints the pooled-vs-FE comparison. The deck therefore reviews the method and reports what the code actually computes.
:::

## Random effects: a team effect assumed unrelated to wins

$$y_{it} = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x_{it} + \underbrace{(\alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it})}_{\text{composite error}}, \qquad \alpha_i \sim (0,\sigma_\alpha^2),\;\; \varepsilon_{it} \sim (0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2)$$

::: {.incremental}
- **Key assumption**: $\text{Cov}(\alpha_i, x_{it}) = 0$, i.e. the team effect is unrelated to the regressor
- **Estimation**: feasible GLS, which *partially* de-means: $y_{it} - \theta\,\bar y_i$ with $\theta = 1 - \sqrt{\sigma_\varepsilon^2 / (\sigma_\varepsilon^2 + T\sigma_\alpha^2)}$
- $\theta = 0$ gives pooled OLS, $\theta = 1$ gives FE; RE sits **in between** and uses some between variation
:::

[RE buys efficiency with an assumption. If big-market teams also win more, the assumption fails and RE inherits part of the pooled bias.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The quasi-demeaning formula is the standard textbook RE (GLS) transformation, added here as a method review; the chapter states only "Feasible GLS". With T = 10 seasons and a large team-effect variance, theta would be close to 1, so RE would land close to FE. That is a statement about the formula, not an estimate: RE is not estimated in the chapter or in this deck.
:::

## Pooled, RE, FE: what each one compares {.smaller}

| | Pooled OLS | Random effects | Fixed effects |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Variation used** | between + within, equal weights | within + a fraction $(1-\theta)$ of between | within only |
| **Assumes about $\alpha_i$** | uncorrelated with $x$ (and ignored) | uncorrelated with $x$ | nothing; may correlate with $x$ |
| **Consistent if $\alpha_i$ correlates with $x$?** | no | no | **yes** |
| **Efficient if it doesn't?** | no | **yes** | no |
| **Time-invariant regressors?** | yes | yes | no |
| **NBA estimate** | 0.00675 | *not estimated* | [0.00451]{.key} |

[In observational panels the "no correlation" assumption is rarely credible, so FE is the default and RE needs a justification.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
RE is typically defensible when the unit effects are plausibly random with respect to the regressor, for example when the regressor is randomly assigned. In the NBA case, market size almost certainly correlates with the ability to buy a winning roster.
:::

## The Hausman test: does RE's assumption survive?

$$H = (\hat\beta_{FE} - \hat\beta_{RE})'\,\big[\widehat V(\hat\beta_{FE}) - \widehat V(\hat\beta_{RE})\big]^{-1}(\hat\beta_{FE} - \hat\beta_{RE}) \;\sim\; \chi^2_k$$

::: {.incremental}
- $H_0$: $\alpha_i$ uncorrelated with the regressors, so **both** are consistent and RE is efficient: the two estimates should be close
- $H_a$: correlated, so only FE is consistent: the estimates diverge
- A large $H$ (small $p$) rejects RE; keep FE
:::

[The chapter states the test but never computes it, so this deck reports **no** Hausman result for the NBA. Treat any claim that "Hausman rejects RE here" as unverified.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The classic Hausman statistic assumes RE is fully efficient under H0, which fails with heteroskedastic or clustered errors; a robust alternative is the correlated-random-effects (Mundlak) test, adding team means of x as regressors. Both are mentioned as standard practice, not estimated.

Fidelity note: the chapter's Key Concepts example says the FE coefficient is "noticeably smaller than the RE coefficient" and that the Hausman test "typically rejects RE". Neither RE nor the test is estimated anywhere in the chapter. Practice Exercise 3 (χ² = 25.4) is a hypothetical, not this dataset.
:::

# 17.4b · Who earns more than \$60,000? {#sec-logit .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Binary outcomes · linear probability model · logit · marginal effects]{.act}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's 17.4 also introduces nonlinear models through a logit. Different data: a cross-section of workers, no panel structure. The lesson: when y is 0/1, read the model through predicted probabilities and marginal effects.
:::

## The question: education, age and the chance of a high income {.smaller}

**Data.** 872 full-time workers, 2010 (`AED_EARNINGS_COMPLETE.DTA`). Outcome: `dbigearn` = 1 if annual earnings exceed \$60,000.

| Variable | Meaning | Mean |
|:--|:--|--:|
| `dbigearn` | 1 if earnings > \$60,000 (238 workers) | 0.273 |
| `education` | years of schooling (0–20) | 13.85 |
| `age` | years | 43.3 |

::: {.incremental}
- **Linear probability model (LPM)**: $\Pr(y=1\mid x) = x'\beta$; slopes are probability changes, but fitted values can leave $[0,1]$
- **Logit**: $\Pr(y=1\mid x) = \dfrac{e^{x'\beta}}{1+e^{x'\beta}}$; always in $(0,1)$, but $\beta_j$ is in **log-odds** units
:::

[Logit's marginal effect $\partial p/\partial x_j = p(1-p)\,\beta_j$ changes with $p$, so you must say *where* you evaluate it.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's datasets list says 842 workers; the file has 872 and all results use 872. The marginal effect is largest at p = 0.5, where it equals β/4, and shrinks toward zero in the tails.
:::

## Code: build the binary outcome and fit the logit

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-7|8|9-10"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                      # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import pandas as pd                           # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                         # OLS for the linear probability model
from statsmodels.formula.api import logit     # logit with R-style formulas
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_EARNINGS_COMPLETE.DTA"
data_earnings = pd.read_stata(url)            # 872 full-time workers, 2010
data_earnings["dbigearn"] = (data_earnings["earnings"] > 60000).astype(int)  # 1 = high earner
print(data_earnings["dbigearn"].mean())       # share of high earners
model_logit = logit("dbigearn ~ age + education", data=data_earnings).fit(cov_type="HC1", disp=0)
print(model_logit.summary())                  # coefficients in log-odds units, robust SEs
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained block. The logit is fitted by maximum likelihood; cov_type="HC1" requests heteroskedasticity-robust (sandwich) standard errors, as in the chapter.
:::

## Output: logit coefficients are log-odds, not probabilities {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | SE | $z$ | $p$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Intercept | −8.0651 | 0.6914 | −11.67 | <&nbsp;0.001 |
| `age` | 0.0385 | 0.0080 | 4.85 | <&nbsp;0.001 |
| `education` | [0.3742]{.key} | 0.0366 | 10.22 | <&nbsp;0.001 |

[N = 872 · share with `dbigearn` = 1: 0.273 · HC1 SEs · McFadden pseudo-$R^2 = 0.145$]{.comment}

::: {.incremental}
- **Sign and significance** read as usual: older and more educated workers are more likely to earn above \$60k
- **Size** does not: one more year of schooling multiplies the **odds** by $e^{0.3742} = 1.45$
- To talk about probabilities we need **marginal effects**
:::

[A logit coefficient of 0.37 is not "37 percentage points". It is a change in log-odds.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Pseudo-R² compares the log likelihood with a constant-only model; it is not a share of variance and is typically much lower than OLS R² values. The odds ratio is the cleanest exact reading of a logit coefficient.
:::

## Code: marginal effects and the linear probability model

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4|5-6|7-8"}
# continues from the previous block
ame = model_logit.get_margeff()               # default at="overall": AVERAGE marginal effects
mem = model_logit.get_margeff(at="mean")      # marginal effects AT THE MEANS of age, education
print(ame.summary()); print(mem.summary())
fit_lpm = pf.feols("dbigearn ~ age + education", data=data_earnings, vcov="HC1")
fit_lpm.summary()                             # slopes are directly probability changes
p_lpm = fit_lpm.predict()                     # LPM fitted "probabilities"
print((p_lpm < 0).sum(), p_lpm.min())         # how many fall below zero?
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
The chapter calls get_margeff() and labels the output "Marginal Effects (at means)". But statsmodels' default is at="overall": it averages each worker's marginal effect (the AME). Marginal effects at the means need at="mean". The deck runs both.
:::

## Output: three answers to "one more year of schooling" {.smaller}

| Effect on $\Pr(\text{earnings} > \$60\text{k})$ | `education` | SE | `age` | SE |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Logit, **average** marginal effect (`get_margeff()`) | [0.0618]{.key} | 0.0047 | 0.0064 | 0.0013 |
| Logit, marginal effect **at the means** (`at="mean"`) | 0.0662 | 0.0062 | 0.0068 | 0.0014 |
| Linear probability model (OLS, HC1) | 0.0540 | 0.0050 | 0.0064 | 0.0013 |

[LPM: N = 872 · $R^2 = 0.142$ · 95% CI for `education` [0.0442, 0.0639]]{.comment}

[One more year of schooling raises the probability of earning above \$60k by about **6.2 percentage points** on average (logit), or 5.4 (LPM). Same sign, similar size.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter's text says the education marginal effect "at the sample means" is "about 0.05, i.e. roughly a 5-percentage-point rise". At the means it is 0.066; the average marginal effect (what the chapter's code actually prints) is 0.062; 0.054 is the LPM coefficient. The qualitative lesson holds (logit and LPM agree on sign and rough size); the numbers need the right labels. The formula check: p at the means = 0.229, so 0.229 × 0.771 × 0.3742 = 0.066.
:::

## Where the two models part ways

![Predicted probability by years of education, age fixed at its mean. Shaded: impossible negative "probabilities".](figures/fig_logit_lpm.png)

[In the data, **30 of 872** LPM fitted values are negative (minimum −0.59). Every logit prediction stays between 0.001 and 0.86.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The two curves agree in the middle of the data (12–16 years of schooling): at 16 years both predict about 0.39–0.40. They diverge in the tails, where the LPM line keeps going and the logit flattens. At 20 years the logit predicts 0.75, the LPM 0.61. The negative LPM predictions come from workers with very little schooling. Average marginal effects summarize the curve with one number; the picture shows why one number hides variation.
:::

## Reading the logit honestly

::: {.incremental}
- **Report marginal effects**, and say which: average (AME) or at the means (MEM). They differ here by 0.004
- **LPM is a fine first pass** for average effects near the middle of the data; use logit (or probit) for predictions and for the tails
- **Association, not return to schooling**: ability, family background and occupation choice correlate with education and with earnings
- The cut-off is arbitrary: \$60,000 discards most of the information in `earnings`, which the log-earnings regressions of earlier chapters use in full
:::

[A binary model changes the *scale* of the answer, not the *identification* problem.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This example sits in the panel chapter only because the chapter places nonlinear models in 17.4. Nothing here is a panel. The identification caveats are the same as for any cross-sectional regression of earnings on education.
:::

# Act II-b · Time series: order and memory {.divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[17.5 – 17.6 · stationarity, spurious regression, HAC, autocorrelation, AR and ADL]{.act}

::: {.notes}
One unit (the U.S. Treasury market), 397 months. The panel problems become time problems: shared trends instead of shared team traits, and serial correlation instead of within-cluster correlation.
:::

# 17.5 · Do long rates follow short rates? {#sec-ts .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Stationarity · spurious regression · levels with a trend · Newey–West HAC]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 17.5: the levels regression of the 10-year Treasury rate on the 1-year rate, with a time trend, under default and HAC standard errors.
:::

## The question and the data {.smaller}

**Data.** Monthly U.S. Treasury yields, January 1982 – January 2015: **397 months** (`AED_INTERESTRATES.DTA`).

| Variable | Meaning | Mean | Range |
|:--|:--|--:|:--|
| `gs10` | 10-year Treasury rate, % | 6.19 | 1.53 – 14.59 |
| `gs1` | 1-year Treasury rate, % | 4.69 | 0.10 – 14.73 |
| `dgs10` | monthly change in `gs10`, percentage points | −0.03 | −1.43 – 0.78 |
| `dgs1` | monthly change in `gs1`, percentage points | −0.04 | −1.81 – 0.76 |

[**Economic question**: how much of a move in short rates (which the Fed influences) passes through to long rates (which matter for mortgages and investment)?]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The expectations hypothesis says long rates reflect expected future short rates, plus a term premium. If so, short-rate moves should pass through to long rates, but less than one-for-one, because a 1-year move changes only part of the expected 10-year path.
:::

## Three time-series ideas to keep in view

::: {.incremental}
- **Autocorrelation** at lag $k$: $r_k = \dfrac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}(y_t-\bar y)(y_{t-k}-\bar y)}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t-\bar y)^2}$. Today resembles yesterday
- **Stationarity**: mean, variance and autocorrelations do not change over time. Trending series are **non-stationary**
- **Spurious regression**: regress one trending series on another and you get a high $R^2$ and huge $t$-statistics even with no structural link
:::

[With trending data a large $R^2$ is a warning, not a reward. Two cures: **difference** the data, or keep levels and use **HAC** standard errors (and think hard).]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Many macro series behave like random walks with drift; their levels wander and their changes are roughly stationary. Spurious regression (Granger and Newbold) is the time-series analogue of confounding by a common factor: here the common factor is time itself.
:::

## Both rates drift down from 14% to near zero

![Monthly 10-year and 1-year Treasury yields, 1982–2015.](figures/fig_rates_levels.png)

[Over 33 years both rates fall by more than ten points. Any regression of one level on the other will partly fit this shared downward drift. In levels the two series correlate 0.95.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Notice also the late period: after 2008 the 1-year rate is pinned near zero (the zero lower bound) while the 10-year rate keeps moving. A single linear relationship across 1982–2015 also assumes the relationship is stable through very different monetary regimes.
:::

## Code: the levels regression, with default and HAC SEs

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-6|7-10|11"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                     # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import numpy as np                           # numerical operations
import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                        # OLS with default / HAC standard errors
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_INTERESTRATES.DTA"
data_rates = pd.read_stata(url)              # 397 months, Jan 1982 – Jan 2015
data_rates["time"] = np.arange(len(data_rates))              # linear time trend 0, 1, 2, ...
fit_levels = pf.feols("gs10 ~ gs1 + time", data=data_rates)   # default SEs
fit_levels_hac = pf.feols("gs10 ~ gs1 + time", data=data_rates, vcov="NW",
                          vcov_kwargs={"time_id": "time", "lag": 24})   # Newey–West, 24 lags
fit_levels_hac.summary()                     # same coefficients, HAC SEs
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained. Including a linear time trend lets the regression absorb a common linear drift, but not wandering, non-linear trends. HAC with 24 lags allows errors to be correlated over two years of monthly data.
:::

## Output: a near-perfect fit, and SEs that were 3.6× too small {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | Default SE | Default $t$ | HAC SE | HAC $t$ | HAC ÷ default |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Intercept | 5.8994 | 0.2254 | 26.17 | 0.6640 | 8.89 | 2.95 |
| `gs1` | [0.5076]{.key} | 0.0221 | 22.92 | 0.0808 | 6.28 | [3.65]{.key} |
| `time` | −0.0106 | 0.0006 | −16.69 | 0.0018 | −5.79 | 2.88 |

[N = 397 · $R^2 = 0.947$ · HAC: Newey–West, 24 lags · HAC 95% CI for `gs1`: [0.3488, 0.6663]]{.comment}

[Holding a linear trend fixed, a 1-point higher short rate goes with a **0.51-point** higher long rate. The fit looks superb, but the residuals are highly persistent, so default SEs overstate precision more than threefold.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Matches the chapter: R² around 0.95 and a HAC SE more than three times the default (3.65×). The time coefficient says the long rate drifted down by about 0.011 points per month (about 0.13 per year) beyond what the short rate explains.

The chapter later claims the "long-run" levels coefficient is "≈ 0.90–0.95". With the trend it is 0.51; without the trend (the chapter's cheat-sheet regression gs10 ~ gs1) it is 0.84, with R² 0.909. Neither is 0.90–0.95.
:::

## How HAC standard errors work

$$\widehat V_{\text{HAC}} = (X'X)^{-1}\Big[\hat\Omega_0 + \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} w_\ell\,\big(\hat\Omega_\ell + \hat\Omega_\ell'\big)\Big](X'X)^{-1}, \qquad w_\ell = 1 - \frac{\ell}{L+1}$$

::: {.incremental}
- $\hat\Omega_\ell = \sum_t \hat u_t \hat u_{t-\ell}\, x_t x_{t-\ell}'$: the covariance of scores $\ell$ months apart
- **Bartlett weights** $w_\ell$ shrink distant lags; $L$ is chosen by the analyst (here 24 months)
- HAC fixes the **standard errors**; it does **not** fix a spurious **coefficient**
:::

[HAC is to time series what clustering is to panels: same sandwich, different idea of which errors may be correlated.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The Newey–West estimator is the cluster-robust sandwich with a different middle: instead of summing within clusters, it sums cross-products of nearby periods with declining weights. Choosing L: rules of thumb such as 0.75·T^(1/3) give about 5.5 for T = 397; the chapter chooses 24 (two years) to be conservative given the strong persistence.
:::

# 17.6 · Autocorrelation: is the levels fit spurious? {#sec-ac .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Correlogram · consequences · first differencing]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Section 17.6: diagnose the residuals of the levels regression, then re-estimate in changes.
:::

## Autocorrelation: what it breaks and how to see it

::: {.incremental}
- **Consequences**: OLS coefficients stay unbiased (if the regressors are exogenous), but default SEs are wrong, usually **too small**, and $t$-tests over-reject
- **Detect**: the **correlogram** of residuals; the Breusch–Godfrey LM test; the Durbin–Watson statistic for AR(1) errors
- **Respond**: HAC SEs; model the dynamics (AR, ADL); or **first-difference** non-stationary series
:::

[A slowly decaying correlogram is the fingerprint of a non-stationary, near-unit-root error.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter imports acorr_breusch_godfrey but never runs it; the deck relies on the correlogram, as the chapter's code does. Approximate 95% band for a single autocorrelation under white noise: ±1.96/√T = ±0.098 here.
:::

## Code: residual autocorrelations of the levels regression

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-5|6-7"}
# continues from the previous block
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf             # autocorrelation function
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf    # correlogram plot
data_rates["uhatgs10"] = fit_levels._u_hat            # residuals of the levels regression
acf_resid = acf(data_rates["uhatgs10"].dropna(), nlags=10)   # lags 0..10
for k in range(11): print(k, round(acf_resid[k], 3)) # lag-1 ≈ 0.95
plot_acf(data_rates["uhatgs10"].dropna(), lags=24, alpha=0.05)  # with a 95% band
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
The residuals of the levels-plus-trend regression are what the trend did not absorb. If they wander, the regression has not captured a stable relationship.
:::

## Output: the residuals barely forget {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
| Lag | $r_k$ |
|:--|--:|
| 1 | [0.953]{.key} |
| 2 | 0.888 |
| 3 | 0.830 |
| 4 | 0.769 |
| 5 | 0.709 |
| 8 | 0.538 |
| 10 | [0.425]{.key} |

[95% band: ±0.098]{.comment}
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
![Correlogram of the levels-regression residuals, lags 1–24.](figures/fig_x_03.png){height="400"}
:::
::::

[Still 0.42 after ten months. Errors this persistent mean the 397 months carry far less independent information than 397 observations, which is why HAC SEs were 3.65× larger.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Matches the chapter: lag 1 = 0.95, lag 10 = 0.42. Every bar is far outside the band. This is the signature of non-stationary (or near unit-root) residuals: the levels relationship may be partly spurious.
:::

## First differences: compare changes with changes

$$\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}, \qquad \Delta\text{gs10}_t = \beta_1 + \beta_2\,\Delta\text{gs1}_t + u_t$$

::: {.incremental}
- Differencing removes a stochastic trend and any linear trend (it becomes the intercept)
- The question changes: "when short rates **move** this month, how much do long rates **move**?"
- Cost: long-run level information is discarded; only month-to-month variation identifies $\beta_2$
:::

[The time-series cousin of fixed effects: drop the persistent component, keep the changes.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The analogy is exact for two-period panels: first differences and fixed effects coincide when T = 2. In both cases, a component that does not change (a team's market, a series' level) is removed so that it cannot confound the slope.
:::

## Monthly changes: no trend, centred on zero

![Monthly changes in the 10-year and 1-year rates, 1982–2015.](figures/fig_rates_changes.png)

[The changes look stationary: no drift, a constant mean near zero, but bursts of volatility (early 1980s, 2008), a reminder to use robust SEs.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Volatility clustering is a form of heteroskedasticity over time. The chapter estimates the changes regression with default SEs; HAC SEs for the same regression are 0.042 instead of 0.031 for dgs1 (computed for these slides), which changes nothing substantive here (t = 17 instead of 23).
:::

## Code: the regression in changes

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-6"}
# continues from the previous block
fit_changes = pf.feols("dgs10 ~ dgs1", data=data_rates)   # regression in first differences
fit_changes.summary()                                    # N = 396 (first month has no change)
uhat_dgs10 = fit_changes._u_hat                          # residuals in changes
acf_dgs10_resid = acf(uhat_dgs10[~np.isnan(uhat_dgs10)], nlags=10)
print(acf_dgs10_resid[1])                                # lag-1 autocorrelation
```

# 17.6b · How fast do short-rate moves reach long rates? {#sec-dyn .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[AR($p$) · ADL($p,q$) · impact and cumulative multipliers]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Still section 17.6 in the chapter (Autoregressive Models). The ADL(2,2) is estimated in the chapter's Key Takeaways code block; the deck runs it as a main result.
:::

## Dynamic models: let the past enter the regression

$$\text{AR}(p):\quad y_t = \beta_0 + \alpha_1 y_{t-1} + \cdots + \alpha_p y_{t-p} + u_t$$

$$\text{ADL}(p,q):\quad y_t = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p}\alpha_j\,y_{t-j} + \sum_{j=0}^{q}\gamma_j\,x_{t-j} + u_t$$

::: {.incremental}
- $\alpha_j$: **persistence** (momentum or reversal) in $y$ itself
- $\gamma_0$: **impact multiplier**, the same-month response to $x$
- $\gamma_0+\gamma_1+\dots$: **cumulative** distributed-lag multipliers; the **long-run multiplier** also accounts for the AR terms: $\sum_j\gamma_j \,/\, (1-\sum_j \alpha_j)$
:::

[Here $y_t = \Delta\text{gs10}_t$ and $x_t = \Delta\text{gs1}_t$: an ADL(2,2) in **changes**.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The long-run multiplier formula is standard for stable ADL models: after a permanent unit change in x, y settles where y = (Σγ/(1−Σα))·x. With y and x in changes, this is the long-run response of the change in the long rate to a sustained change in the change of the short rate. Students should mainly read the impact and cumulative sums.
:::

## Code: build lags and fit the ADL(2,2)

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-7|8-9|10"}
# continues from the previous block
for k in [1, 2]:                                       # lags with .shift(k)
    data_rates[f"dgs10_lag{k}"] = data_rates["dgs10"].shift(k)
    data_rates[f"dgs1_lag{k}"] = data_rates["dgs1"].shift(k)
fit_adl = pf.feols("dgs10 ~ dgs10_lag1 + dgs10_lag2 + dgs1 + dgs1_lag1 + dgs1_lag2",
                   data=data_rates)                    # ADL(2,2), N = 394
fit_adl.summary()                                      # default SEs, as in the chapter
c = fit_adl.coef()                                     # cumulative pass-through:
print(c["dgs1"], c["dgs1"] + c["dgs1_lag1"], c["dgs1"] + c["dgs1_lag1"] + c["dgs1_lag2"])
print(acf(pd.Series(fit_adl._u_hat).dropna(), nlags=1)[1])   # residual lag-1 autocorrelation
```

::: {.notes}
Three months are lost to the lags (one for the difference, two for the second lag), leaving 394. The code is the chapter's Key Takeaways cheat-sheet block.
:::

## Output: strong impact, partial reversal, positive momentum {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | SE | $t$ | $p$ | 95% CI |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Intercept | −0.0067 | 0.0088 | −0.76 | 0.447 | [−0.0239,&nbsp;0.0106] |
| `dgs10_lag1` | 0.2830 | 0.0508 | 5.57 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.1831,&nbsp;0.3828] |
| `dgs10_lag2` | −0.1021 | 0.0506 | −2.02 | 0.044 | [−0.2015,&nbsp;−0.0027] |
| `dgs1` | [0.7397]{.key} | 0.0340 | 21.74 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.6728,&nbsp;0.8066] |
| `dgs1_lag1` | −0.2588 | 0.0514 | −5.03 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [−0.3599,&nbsp;−0.1576] |
| `dgs1_lag2` | 0.0515 | 0.0492 | 1.05 | 0.296 | [−0.0453,&nbsp;0.1482] |

[N = 394 · default SEs · $R^2 = 0.611$ · residual lag-1 autocorrelation 0.008]{.comment}

[Same month: **0.74** points of pass-through. Next month a **partial reversal** (−0.26). The long rate's own lagged change enters **positively** (+0.28): momentum, not mean reversion.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
These are the chapter's Key Concept numbers (≈ +0.28, γ0 ≈ 0.74, γ1 ≈ −0.26, γ2 ≈ 0.05, two-month multiplier ≈ 0.53). The chapter's longer narrative under "Typical ADL(2,2) Results" contradicts them: it gives γ0 ≈ 0.45–0.55, γ1 ≈ +0.15 to +0.25, γ2 ≈ +0.05 to +0.10, a total of ≈ 0.78, R² ≈ 0.40–0.50, and says the coefficient on the lagged change is negative (mean reversion). The estimates above are what the data give. HAC SEs (computed for these slides) leave every conclusion unchanged: γ0 t = 14.0, γ1 t = −4.33, γ2 p = 0.26.
:::

## Pass-through, month by month

![Cumulative distributed-lag multipliers from the ADL(2,2).](figures/fig_adl_multipliers.png)

[About **0.74** of a 1-point short-rate change shows up in the long rate at once; after the partial reversal, **0.53** has passed through within two months.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Cumulative sums of the γ coefficients: 0.740, 0.481, 0.532. Including the autoregressive terms, the long-run multiplier is 0.532 / (1 − 0.283 + 0.102) = 0.65 (computed for these slides). All are well below one-for-one, consistent with the expectations hypothesis: a change in the 1-year rate moves only part of the expected path of short rates over ten years.
:::

## Did the dynamics soak up the autocorrelation?

![Residual autocorrelations, lags 1–24, for three specifications. Shaded band: ±1.96/√T.](figures/fig_acf_compare.png)

[Levels: 0.95. Static changes: 0.25. ADL(2,2): **0.01**. Modelling the dynamics leaves residuals that look like white noise.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Left to right, the specifications climb from a spurious-looking levels fit to a well-specified dynamic model. A few isolated bars still touch the band at long lags; with 24 lags, one or two crossings are expected by chance at the 5% level.
:::

## Code: compare static, AR(2) and ADL(2,2) on one sample

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-8"}
# continues from the previous block (computed for these slides)
samp = data_rates.dropna(subset=["dgs10_lag2", "dgs1_lag2"])    # same 394 months for all
models = {"static": "dgs10 ~ dgs1", "AR(2)": "dgs10 ~ dgs10_lag1 + dgs10_lag2",
          "ADL(2,2)": "dgs10 ~ dgs10_lag1 + dgs10_lag2 + dgs1 + dgs1_lag1 + dgs1_lag2"}
for name, fml in models.items():
    f = pf.feols(fml, data=samp); n, k = f._N, len(f.coef())
    bic = n * np.log((f._u_hat ** 2).sum() / n) + k * np.log(n)   # lower is better
    print(name, round(f._r2, 3), round(acf(pd.Series(f._u_hat), nlags=1)[1], 3), round(bic, 1))
```

## Output: the ADL wins on every criterion

| Model | $R^2$ | Residual lag-1 $\rho$ | BIC |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Static: $\Delta$gs10 on $\Delta$gs1 | 0.573 | 0.259 | −1346.8 |
| AR(2): own lags only | 0.125 | 0.012 | −1057.9 |
| ADL(2,2) | [0.611]{.key} | [0.008]{.key} | [−1359.7]{.key} |

::: {.notes}
The chapter's comparison table (0.57 / 0.25, 0.13 / 0.01, 0.61 / 0.01, with BIC "Higher/Lower") is confirmed; the BIC values are computed here on a common sample of 394 months so that they are comparable. Note what each part buys: own lags alone explain little (R² 0.125) but whiten the residuals; the short rate explains most of the variation; together, the ADL wins on every criterion. The ADL's R² gain over the static model is modest (0.038).
:::

## Reading time-series regressions with care

::: {.incremental}
- **Units**: changes are in **percentage points**, not percent. "A 1% rise in the 1-year rate" should read "a 1-percentage-point rise"
- **Levels vs changes answer different questions**: equilibrium co-movement vs monthly pass-through
- **Stability**: one set of coefficients spans 1982–2015, including the zero-lower-bound years after 2008
- **Not causal by default**: both rates respond to the same news (inflation, growth); the ADL describes **predictive** dynamics and transmission, not a controlled experiment
:::

[A time-series regression is credible when its residuals are white noise *and* its story survives a check of stability and common shocks.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Corrections applied in the slides: the chapter's overshooting example ("Fed raises 1-year rate by 1%") uses percent where it means percentage points, and its numbers (0.60, −0.10, −0.02, settling at 0.85) are illustrative, not estimates. Cointegration and unit-root tests are the formal tools for the levels question (named in the chapter's Next Steps), not used here.
:::

The deck reviews the concepts and then points to the Chapter 13 deck, where an RCT, a difference-in-differences, a regression discontinuity and an instrumental-variables design are each estimated on real data.

# 17.7 · When is a slope causal? {#sec-causal .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Concepts only · worked designs in the Chapter 13 deck]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Bridge from the panel and time-series sections: FE removed time-invariant confounders and differencing removed trends, but neither guarantees that the remaining variation in x is as good as random.
:::

## OLS is biased the moment $x$ is correlated with the error

$$y = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x + u, \qquad \text{OLS is consistent only if } E[u \mid x] = 0$$

::: {.incremental}
- **Omitted variables**: a confounder drives both $x$ and $y$. *NBA*: market size raises revenue and buys wins (FE removed the time-invariant part)
- **Measurement error** in $x$: attenuates the slope toward zero
- **Simultaneity / reverse causation**: $y$ also moves $x$. *NBA*: revenue pays for players, players produce wins
:::

[Adding controls fixes only the confounders you **measure**. Credible causal claims need an **identification strategy**.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Each source has a different direction of bias. Omitted variables can go either way (sign of the OVB formula); classical measurement error biases toward zero; simultaneity depends on the feedback. Fixed effects address only one specific form of omitted variable: the time-invariant one.
:::

## Potential outcomes: what a causal effect means

$$\text{individual effect} = Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}, \qquad \text{ATE} = E[Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}]$$

::: {.incremental}
- $Y_{1i}$: the outcome **if treated**; $Y_{0i}$: the outcome **if not**. Only one is ever observed
- A naive comparison of treated and untreated: $E[Y_1\mid D{=}1] - E[Y_0\mid D{=}0] = \text{ATT} + \underbrace{E[Y_0\mid D{=}1]-E[Y_0\mid D{=}0]}_{\text{selection bias}}$
- Every design is a way to make the selection-bias term zero, or to remove it
:::

[A causal estimate is a claim about a **counterfactual**. The design is the argument for why your comparison group stands in for it.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter defines potential outcomes and the ATE; the decomposition into ATT plus selection bias is the standard result (added as method review, and worked through with data in the Chapter 13 deck's Act II-b).
:::

## Instrumental variables: borrow variation that is as good as random {.smaller}

An instrument $z$ must satisfy two conditions:

::: {.incremental}
- **Relevance**: $\text{Cov}(z, x) \neq 0$. *Testable*: first-stage $F$ (rule of thumb $> 10$)
- **Exogeneity / exclusion**: $\text{Cov}(z, u) = 0$, so $z$ affects $y$ **only through** $x$. *Not testable*: must be argued
:::

. . .

With one regressor and one instrument, substitute $y = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x + u$ into $\text{Cov}(z, y)$:

$$\text{Cov}(z,y) = \beta_2\,\text{Cov}(z,x) + \underbrace{\text{Cov}(z,u)}_{=\,0} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \hat\beta_{IV} = \frac{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z,y)}{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(z,x)} = \frac{\text{reduced form}}{\text{first stage}}$$

[IV is consistent where OLS is not, but only for the variation the instrument moves (a *local* effect), and only as good as the exclusion argument.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The derivation shows exactly where each condition enters: exogeneity kills the Cov(z,u) term; relevance makes the denominator non-zero. A weak first stage (small Cov(z,x)) magnifies any small violation of exogeneity. In pyfixest the syntax is pf.feols("y ~ 1 | x ~ z", data=...); a worked example with data is in the Chapter 13 deck (case 13.8).
:::

## The causal toolkit {.smaller}

| Method | Source of variation | Identifying assumption | Where to see it worked |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Randomized experiment | random assignment | randomization intact (no attrition bias) | [Ch 13.5 · RAND HIE](../ch13/index.html#/case-135){data-preview-link="false"} |
| Fixed effects | within-unit changes | no **time-varying** confounders | this deck, [17.3](#sec-fe), [CS 1](#cs-1), [CS 2](#cs-2) |
| Difference-in-differences | group × period | parallel trends | [Ch 13.6 · South Africa](../ch13/index.html#/case-136){data-preview-link="false"} |
| Regression discontinuity | a cutoff in a running variable | continuity at the cutoff | [Ch 13.7 · U.S. Senate](../ch13/index.html#/case-137){data-preview-link="false"} |
| Instrumental variables | an instrument | relevance + exclusion | [Ch 13.8 · institutions](../ch13/index.html#/case-138){data-preview-link="false"} |
| Matching / propensity scores | observed covariates | selection on observables only | (named in the chapter; not worked) |

[Every row trades the unverifiable "I controlled for everything" for a specific assumption you can defend, probe, or attack.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Links open the Chapter 13 deck at the corresponding case. Fixed effects belong in this table: they are a design, not just an estimator. Their assumption (no time-varying confounders) is weaker than "no confounders" but still an assumption.
:::

## The worked designs: naive vs design, from the Chapter 13 deck {.smaller}

| Ch 13 case | Design | Naive comparison | Design-based estimate |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| [13.5](../ch13/index.html#/case-135){data-preview-link="false"} | RCT (health insurance) | *(randomized: no naive version needed)* | 95% plan: [−\$1,108]{.key} vs free care |
| [13.6](../ch13/index.html#/case-136){data-preview-link="false"} | DiD (child nutrition) | treated before vs after: +0.867 | [+0.522]{.key} z-units |
| [13.7](../ch13/index.html#/case-137){data-preview-link="false"} | RD (Senate incumbency) | winners vs losers: +21.7 pp | [+4.8 pp]{.key} |
| [13.8](../ch13/index.html#/case-138){data-preview-link="false"} | IV (institutions) | OLS: 0.52 | 2SLS: [0.94]{.key} |

[Same lesson as pooled vs FE in this chapter: when the comparison changes, the number changes, sometimes by a factor of four.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Numbers quoted from the verified Chapter 13 deck (see its synthesis act); nothing is re-estimated here. Pair them with this chapter's own contrasts: NBA pooled 0.0068 vs FE 0.0045; capital elasticity pooled 0.71 vs FE 0.44; population slope pooled +0.34 vs FE −0.82.
:::

## Practical recommendations from 17.7

::: {.incremental}
- Name the **confounders** before running anything; ask which are time-invariant
- **Cluster** (panels) or use **HAC** (time series): honest SEs are part of a credible claim
- **Report several specifications**: pooled and FE, OLS and IV, levels and changes. The *pattern* of changes is evidence
- **State the identifying assumption** in one sentence, and say what would violate it
:::

[A design earns a causal claim; a significant $t$-statistic does not.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
These are the chapter's practical recommendations, with the deck's thread added: the comparison across specifications is not a robustness ritual, it is the main diagnostic.
:::

# Case Study 1 · Does capital raise productivity, within countries? {#cs-1 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[108 countries × 25 years · variance decomposition · cluster SEs · FE · two-way FE · regions]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Mendez (2020) convergence-clubs data. Research question from the chapter: how do physical and human capital relate to labor productivity across countries, and does controlling for unobserved country characteristics change the estimates?
:::

## The question and the data {.smaller}

**Data.** Mendez (2020) convergence-clubs panel: **108 countries × 1990–2014 = 2,700** country-years (balanced).

| Variable | Meaning | Mean | Range |
|:--|:--|--:|:--|
| `ln_lp` | log labor productivity (output per worker) | 9.80 | 6.90 – 11.94 |
| `ln_kl` | log physical capital per worker | 10.76 | 6.59 – 13.22 |
| `h` | human capital index (schooling-based) | 2.99 | 1.32 – 5.20 |
| `region` | Africa 26 · Americas 22 · Asia 28 · Europe 30 · Oceania 2 countries | | |

$$\ln lp_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_k \ln kl_{it} + \beta_h\, h_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}$$

[**Correction.** The chapter's variable list and Task 1 code use `rk` and `hc`, which do not exist in this file (the code stops with a `KeyError`). The columns are `kl` and `h`; the slides use them throughout.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Same file as the Mendez case studies of earlier chapters, where kl and h are used correctly. The chapter's list also names rgdppc and tfp; the file's columns are GDPpc and TFP. With logs on both sides, beta_k is an elasticity; h enters in levels, so beta_h is a semi-elasticity.
:::

## Task 1 · Code: panel structure and variance decomposition

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|3-6|7|8-11"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                         # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, pyfixest as pf # numerics, tables, regressions
base = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/mendez2020-convergence-clubs-code-data/"
dat = pd.read_csv(base + "master/assets/dat.csv")    # 108 countries × 1990–2014
dat["ln_lp"] = np.log(dat["lp"])                     # log labor productivity
dat["ln_kl"] = np.log(dat["kl"])                     # log capital per worker (chapter: "rk")
print(dat["country"].nunique(), dat["year"].nunique(), len(dat))   # 108 25 2700
overall_var = dat["ln_lp"].var()                                    # all country-years
between_var = dat.groupby("country")["ln_lp"].mean().var()          # 108 country means
within_var = dat.groupby("country")["ln_lp"].apply(lambda x: x - x.mean()).var()
print(overall_var, between_var, within_var, between_var / overall_var)
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained, and identical to the chapter's Task 1 code except for the corrected column name. Variances rather than SDs, as in the chapter's task.
:::

## Task 1 · Output: 95% of the variation is between countries

| | Variance of `ln_lp` | Share |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Overall (2,700 country-years) | 1.391 | 100% |
| Between (108 country means) | [1.328]{.key} | [95.4%]{.key} |
| Within (deviations from own mean) | 0.075 | 5.4% |

[Shares need not sum to exactly 100%: the between variance is computed over 108 means, the within variance over 2,700 deviations.]{.comment}

[Productivity differences are overwhelmingly **permanent cross-country gaps**. Pooled OLS will be driven by them; fixed effects will keep only the 5% that moves within countries.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Answer to the task's question: the between component dominates far more than in the NBA (81%). Implication: pooled OLS and FE answer very different questions. Pooled: are capital-rich countries more productive? FE: when a country accumulates capital, does its productivity rise?
:::

## Task 2 · Code: pooled OLS with default, robust and cluster SEs

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-6|7-8"}
# continues from the previous block
fit_default = pf.feols("ln_lp ~ ln_kl + h", data=dat)                          # iid SEs
fit_hc1 = pf.feols("ln_lp ~ ln_kl + h", data=dat, vcov="HC1")                  # robust
fit_cluster = pf.feols("ln_lp ~ ln_kl + h", data=dat, vcov={"CRV1": "country"})  # by country
print(pd.DataFrame({"default": fit_default.se(), "HC1": fit_hc1.se(),
                    "cluster": fit_cluster.se()}).round(4))   # same coefficients, three SEs
print((fit_cluster.se() / fit_default.se()).round(2))         # inflation factor
fit_cluster.summary()
```

The chapter's Task 2 code, with ln_kl and h. HC1 is added so the comparison separates heteroskedasticity from within-country dependence.

## Task 2 · Output: clustering quadruples the standard errors {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | Default SE | HC1 SE | Cluster SE | Cluster ÷ default | $t$ (default → cluster) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Intercept | 1.6949 | 0.0581 | 0.0724 | 0.2716 | 4.67 | 29.15 → 6.24 |
| `ln_kl` | [0.7136]{.key} | 0.0081 | 0.0089 | 0.0327 | [4.03]{.key} | 87.74 → 21.79 |
| `h` | 0.1410 | 0.0148 | 0.0150 | 0.0612 | [4.12]{.key} | 9.50 → 2.30 |

[N = 2,700 · 108 country clusters · $R^2 = 0.908$ · cluster 95% CI: `ln_kl` [0.6487, 0.7785], `h` [0.0196, 0.2623] ($p = 0.023$)]{.comment}

[25 years of one country are nearly one observation's worth of evidence about its *level*: clustering inflates SEs about **4×**. `h` drops from $t = 9.5$ to a borderline $t = 2.3$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Answer to the task's question: cluster SEs are about four times the default, much more than the 1.8× in the NBA panel, because country residuals are extremely persistent (95% of variation is between countries, and annual data are smooth). Heteroskedasticity alone (HC1) changes little.
:::

## Task 3 · Code: country fixed effects

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-5"}
# continues from the previous block
fit_fe = pf.feols("ln_lp ~ ln_kl + h | country", data=dat,
                  vcov={"CRV1": "country"})          # one intercept per country
fit_fe.summary()                                     # within-country estimates
print(pd.DataFrame({"pooled": fit_cluster.coef(), "FE": fit_fe.coef()}))   # side by side
```

## Task 3 · Output: capital's elasticity falls by 39% within countries {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | SE | $t$ | $p$ | 95% CI |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| `ln_kl` | [0.4377]{.key} | 0.0377 | 11.61 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.3630,&nbsp;0.5125] |
| `h` | 0.2226 | 0.0566 | 3.93 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.1104,&nbsp;0.3348] |

[N = 2,700 · 108 country fixed effects · CRV1 by country · within $R^2 = 0.670$ · computed for these slides]{.comment}

::: {.incremental}
- **`ln_kl`**: pooled 0.714 → FE **0.438**. Within a country, 1% more capital per worker goes with about 0.44% more output per worker
- **`h`**: pooled 0.141 → FE **0.223**. One more unit of the index: $100(e^{0.2226}-1) = 25\%$ higher productivity
:::

[The capital slope behaves like the NBA case (a positive confounder removed). Human capital moves the **other way**: FE does not always shrink coefficients.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Which coefficients change most, and why: the capital elasticity falls by 39%, consistent with positive omitted-variable bias from persistent country traits (institutions, geography, technology levels) that raise both capital per worker and productivity. The human capital coefficient rises, so the time-invariant confounders were correlated with h in the opposite direction relative to productivity, given capital. The chapter's Key Concept 17.9 says "the typical finding is that FE coefficients are smaller than pooled OLS"; here that holds for capital but not for human capital.
:::

## Pooled vs FE vs two-way FE at a glance

![Coefficients with 95% CIs (clustered by country) under three specifications.](figures/fig_cs1_coefs.png)

[Capital's elasticity is stable once country effects are in (0.44 → 0.40). Human capital's is not: adding year effects makes it **insignificant**.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Read across specifications as the thread suggests. ln_kl: 0.714 (pooled), 0.438 (country FE), 0.401 (country and year FE). h: 0.141, 0.223, 0.103 (p = 0.18). The human capital index trends upward almost everywhere, so once common year effects absorb global trends, little independent within-country variation in h is left.
:::

                    vcov={"CRV1": "country"})       # two-way FE: country AND year
fit_twfe.summary()
fit_trend = pf.feols("ln_lp ~ ln_kl + h + year | country", data=dat,
                     vcov={"CRV1": "country"})      # a common linear trend instead
fit_trend.summary()
year_fe = fit_twfe.fixef()                          # estimated year effects (1990 = 0)

## Task 4 · The common year effects

The 1990s trough (about −0.07 in 1994) partly reflects the transition economies in the sample; the 2009 dip is the global financial crisis. By 2014 the common effect is about +0.07 log points relative to 1990. These are conditional on capital and human capital, so they are a residual "common TFP" path, not total growth.

## Task 4 · Code: do regions grow at different rates? Is there convergence?

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-8|9-12"}
# continues from the previous block (computed for these slides)
dat["t"] = dat["year"] - 1990                                    # years since 1990
fit_rt = pf.feols("ln_lp ~ ln_kl + h + i(region, t) | country", data=dat, vcov={"CRV1": "country"})
names = fit_rt.coef().index; rt = [k for k in names if k.startswith("region::")]
R = np.zeros((len(rt) - 1, len(names)))                           # H0: all trends = Africa's
for j, k in enumerate(rt[1:]):
    R[j, names.get_loc(k)], R[j, names.get_loc(rt[0])] = 1, -1
print(fit_rt.coef()[rt]); print(fit_rt.wald_test(R=R))           # Wald chi2(4)
first = dat[dat["year"] == 1990].set_index("country")["ln_lp"]   # initial productivity
last = dat[dat["year"] == 2014].set_index("country")["ln_lp"]
conv = pd.DataFrame({"ln_lp0": first, "g": 100 * (last - first) / 24}).reset_index()
pf.feols("g ~ ln_lp0", data=conv, vcov="HC1").summary()          # growth on initial level
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
The task asks to "test whether productivity growth rates differ across regions" and "is there evidence of convergence". i(region, t) gives each region its own linear trend (region-time interactions, as the hint suggests), with country FE. Convergence: regress average annual growth 1990–2014 on initial log productivity (a simple cross-country regression; growth in % per year uses the log-difference approximation).
:::

The convergence slope of −0.22 means a country with 1 log point lower productivity in 1990 grew only 0.22 percentage points a year faster, and that difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero. Average annual growth by region (raw, not conditional): Asia 3.25%, Europe 2.67%, Americas 2.23%, Africa 1.41%, Oceania 1.33%.

## Task 5 · Code: do returns to capital differ by region?

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|3-5|6-8"}
# continues from the previous block (computed for these slides)
fit_r1 = pf.feols("ln_lp ~ ln_kl + h + C(region)", data=dat, vcov={"CRV1": "country"})
fit_r2 = pf.feols("ln_lp ~ ln_kl + h + C(region) + C(region):ln_kl + C(region):h",
                  data=dat, vcov={"CRV1": "country"})    # region-specific slopes
fit_r1.summary(); fit_r2.summary()
inter = [k for k in fit_r2.coef().index if ":" in k]     # the 8 interaction terms
R = np.array([[1.0 * (k == a) for k in fit_r2.coef().index] for a in inter])
print(fit_r2.wald_test(R=R))                             # H0: all 8 interactions = 0
```

:::

Which region shows the highest return to human capital? The Americas (0.29) and Africa (0.26), but the h interactions are imprecise (the Asia interaction has p = 0.13), so the ranking is not reliable. These are pooled cross-country associations, subject to all the confounding that Task 3 revealed.

## Task 6 · The policy brief, in numbers {.smaller}

| Specification | `ln_kl` | `h` | Variation used |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| Pooled OLS, cluster SEs | 0.714 (0.033) | 0.141 (0.061) | between + within |
| Country FE | [0.438]{.key} (0.038) | 0.223 (0.057) | within country |
| Country + year FE | 0.401 (0.043) | 0.103 (0.077) | within country, net of common shocks |
| Region-specific slopes (pooled) | 0.64 – 0.78 | −0.08 – 0.29 | between + within, by region |

::: {.incremental}
- **Channels**: capital accumulation is robustly associated with productivity within countries (elasticity ≈ 0.4); the human-capital link is fragile once common trends are removed
- **Causal?** Not established: capital responds to expected productivity (reverse causality), and time-varying policies and shocks remain
:::

[Policy reading: investment climates that raise capital per worker are the best-supported channel in these data, and pooled cross-country estimates overstate it by about 40%.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The task asks for a 200–300 word brief. This slide gives its evidence base. Threats to identification: reverse causality (more productive economies attract investment), measurement error in capital stocks (built by perpetual inventory, which smooths within variation), and the human capital index trending smoothly. The chapter's Key Concept 17.10 adds that the estimator choice should follow the question; here the within estimates are the relevant ones for "what happens when a country accumulates capital".
:::

# Case Study 2 · Night lights and population in Bolivia {#cs-2 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[339 municipalities × 2012–2020 · reshaping · pooled · FE · year effects · first differences]{.act}

::: {.notes}
DS4Bolivia: the final DS4Bolivia case study of the book. The cross-sectional satellite-development data become a panel because nighttime lights and population are available annually for 2012–2020.
:::

## The question and the data {.smaller}

**Data.** DS4Bolivia (`ds4bolivia_v20250523.csv`): **339 municipalities**, annual columns `ln_NTLpc2012` … `ln_NTLpc2020` and `pop2012` … `pop2020`, stored **wide** (one row per municipality).

| Variable | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `ln_NTLpc` | log nighttime lights **per capita** (outcome) |
| `ln_pop` | log population |
| `year` | 2012, …, 2020 |
| `asdf_id`, `mun`, `dep` | municipality id, name, department (9 departments) |

$$\ln NTLpc_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta\,\ln pop_{it} + \delta_t + \varepsilon_{it}$$

[**Research question**: how does luminosity evolve within municipalities over time, and how does it move with population once fixed local traits (altitude, remoteness, climate) are removed?]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key interpretive point for later: the outcome is lights per capita, ln(NTL) − ln(pop). So the coefficient on ln_pop equals (elasticity of total lights with respect to population) − 1. A coefficient of zero would mean total lights grow one-for-one with population.
:::

## Task 1 · Code: reshape wide → long

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-8|9-11"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                         # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, pyfixest as pf # numerics, tables, regressions
url_bol = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/ds4bolivia/master/ds4bolivia_v20250523.csv"
bol = pd.read_csv(url_bol)                       # 339 municipalities, wide format
years = range(2012, 2021)                        # nine annual observations
ntl_long = bol[["mun", "dep", "asdf_id"] + [f"ln_NTLpc{y}" for y in years]].melt(
    id_vars=["mun", "dep", "asdf_id"], var_name="ntl_var", value_name="ln_NTLpc")
ntl_long["year"] = ntl_long["ntl_var"].str.extract(r"(\d{4})").astype(int)  # "…2015" → 2015
pop_long = bol[["asdf_id"] + [f"pop{y}" for y in years]].melt(
    id_vars=["asdf_id"], var_name="pop_var", value_name="pop")
pop_long["year"] = pop_long["pop_var"].str.extract(r"(\d{4})").astype(int)
```
